course.title: GEO 110 Midterm 1
course.bank_intro: Three questions per item, drawn from the concept pages. Answer cold before rereading the page.
course.tracker_intro: Tracks the four Midterm 1 items from first pre-test to mastered.
course.loop:
1. Pre-test each item cold in the quiz.
2. Reread the page for anything under 80%.
3. Post-test with new questions at least a day later.
4. Repeat until every item is mastered.
course.grading: Two parts per question: the answer is marked Y or N, and the reasoning is scored 1–5 (3 is a pass). An attempt passes at 80% on both.

plan.head: Post-test anything not mastered
items: Post-test every weak or shaky item

course.schedule_note: Leave the week before the exam for post-tests only.

quiz.heading: Earth materials pre-tests
quiz.subject: GEO 110, an introductory earth-materials course (rocks, minerals, relative dating, plate tectonics)

items.title: Rock cycle
items.logic: Name the process: cooling from melt is igneous, deposition is sedimentary, solid-state change is metamorphic.

questions.stem: Basalt has very small crystals. What does that say about how it formed?
options: It cooled quickly at the surface
It was changed by heat without melting
questions.why: Fast cooling at the surface leaves no time for large crystals to grow.

questions.stem: Shale is heated and squeezed deep in the crust but never melts. What does it become?
questions.why: Solid-state change by heat and pressure is metamorphism, and shale becomes slate.

questions.stem: If a metamorphic rock melts and the melt cools, the result is still metamorphic rock.
questions.why: Rock that crystallises from melt is igneous, whatever it was before.

items.title: Mohs hardness
items.logic: A mineral scratches anything lower on the scale; the numbers are an order, not a ratio.

questions.stem: A mineral scratches glass but is scratched by quartz. Which could it be?
questions.why: Glass is about 5.5 and quartz 7, so it lies between: orthoclase at 6.

questions.stem: Your fingernail scratches a mineral. Which is it most likely to be?
questions.why: A fingernail is about 2.5, so it only scratches minerals below that, like gypsum at 2.

questions.stem: Diamond (10) is exactly twice as hard as fluorite (5).
questions.why: The Mohs scale is ordinal: it ranks minerals but says nothing about ratios.

items.title: Superposition
items.logic: Undisturbed layers get younger upwards; anything that cuts a layer is younger than it.

questions.stem: A fault cuts layers A (bottom), B and C (top) but not layer D above them. Which order is right, oldest first?
questions.why: The fault cuts A–C so it is younger than them, and D is undisturbed so it came after the fault.

questions.stem: Superposition tells you a layer is 40 million years old.
questions.why: Superposition gives relative ages only; ages in years need radiometric dating.

questions.stem: You find sedimentary layers tilted at 45°. What does original horizontality tell you?
options: They were deposited on a slope
They were tilted after they formed
The top layer is the oldest
questions.why: Sediment is laid down flat, so tilting happened after deposition.

items.title: Plate boundaries
items.logic: Ask whether the plates move apart, together or past each other, and what happens to crust.

questions.stem: Where is new oceanic crust made?
questions.why: At divergent margins such as mid-ocean ridges, rising magma forms new crust.

questions.stem: Oceanic crust meets continental crust at a convergent margin. What happens?
questions.why: Oceanic crust is denser, so it sinks beneath the continent.

questions.stem: Crust is neither created nor destroyed at a transform boundary.
questions.why: At transform margins the plates slide past each other without making or consuming crust.
